sources.title: TodoMVC behavior reference: precise functional contract

model.vision: A simple, dependable todo list that a small team can start relying on tomorrow.

objectives.statement: Let any team member capture, correct, complete, and discard their own tasks with no training or setup, so the team can adopt it the day it ships.
Ensure no one ever loses their todos between visits: a list is exactly as they left it after closing the app, reloading, or restarting their machine.
Keep each person focused on what remains to be done by letting them clear the decks in one step, sweep away finished work, review the list the way they prefer, and always see how much is left.
Let the team's agent tooling manage todos on the same footing as people, so automated workflows can drive the list without a human in the loop.
Put the todo experience wherever the team already works, both as a standalone web experience and embedded alongside the team's other MCP-hosted tools.

model.mission: Reproduce the familiar, well-understood TodoMVC experience faithfully rather than inventing a new one, keep every list safely on the team's side rather than on the user's device, and offer exactly the same todo actions to people and to the team's agents alike.

items.definition: A person on the team who keeps their own todo list and works through it day to day.
The team's automated tooling acting on a team member's todo list with exactly the same actions a person has, without a human in the loop.
The single team member (or the agent acting for them) whose todo list is being viewed or changed; each list belongs to exactly one owner.
One task on a list owner's todo list, made up of a title and a completed state.
The free-text wording of a todo that says what the task is; never blank.
Whether a todo is done (completed) or still to do (active).
A todo that is not yet done.
A todo that has been marked done.
Put a new, active todo with the given title at the end of the list; a blank title adds nothing.
Change an existing todo's title in place, keeping its identity and completed state; finishing an edit with a blank title discards the todo instead.
Abandon an edit in progress so the todo keeps its original title.
Remove one todo from the list, whatever its completed state, leaving every other todo untouched.
Mark one todo as done without affecting any other todo.
Mark one completed todo as still to do without affecting any other todo.
In one action, mark every todo done, or — when every todo is already done — mark every todo as still to do.
In one action, remove every completed todo from the list, leaving active todos untouched; does nothing when none are completed.
The list owner's chosen way of reviewing the list — All, Active, or Completed — which changes only which todos are shown, never the todos themselves.
Show every todo regardless of completed state.
Show only active todos.
Show only completed todos.
The live count of active todos on the whole list, regardless of which filter is chosen.
Guarantee that a list owner finds the same todos, with the same titles and completed states, every time they return, however the previous visit ended.
Deciding whether a submitted title is usable, treating empty or whitespace-only wording as blank.
Deciding which way toggle all goes: mark everything done when any todo is active, otherwise mark everything still to do.
Deciding which todos belong in the view for the chosen filter based on their completed state.
Working out how many todos on the whole list are still active.
Durably append a new active todo with its title to the owner's list.
Durably replace one todo's title.
Durably take one todo off the owner's list.
Durably mark one todo done or still to do.
Durably mark every todo on the owner's list done, or every todo still to do, as one change.
Durably remove every completed todo from the owner's list as one change.
Retrieve the owner's whole todo list, in order, exactly as last kept.
The ordered collection of one list owner's todos.
Where every owner's todo list is kept on the team's side, not on anyone's device, so it survives closing the app, reloading, or restarting a machine.

model.rationale: recommend DecompressedSolution: lowest in-band composite risk (0.581) at 140.0 days (App C risk-crossover exclusions applied)

items.name: Access-channel volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the set of channels through which team members and agents reach the same todo actions. Today there are four (an ordinary web app, an embedded MCP Apps surface, a web API, and MCP tools), and the founder asked for them because that is 'the way we build everything else here'. WHY volatile: the team's tooling conventions are already multi-channel and still moving: MCP itself is young, new agent runtimes keep appearing, and chat, CLI or mobile entry points are the usual next asks for a team tool. LIKELIHOOD: high. At least one channel will be added or reshaped each year over the system's life. EFFECT if unencapsulated: every todo action (add, edit, discard, complete, toggle all, clear completed, filter, count) would be re-implemented per channel, and the guarantee that people and agents get exactly the same actions (the mission) would drift with each new surface. The channel must be a thin, replaceable edge over one shared set of todo actions.

items.name: List-keeping volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: where and how each owner's todo list is durably kept on the team's side, meaning the storage technology, its hosting, and its retention and backup arrangements. WHY volatile: the founder demands a real backend that survives reloads and restarts but deliberately leaves the shape and the store open. A team trialling a tool 'tomorrow' typically starts on a simple store and moves to the team's standard managed database once the tool sticks. LIKELIHOOD: medium-high. At least one change of store or hosting is expected within the first one to three years. EFFECT if unencapsulated: every durable change (record, retitle, remove, set completion, set-all, sweep, recall) would carry storage-specific code, and a store migration would ripple through every workflow and break the keep-list-between-visits guarantee. Storage must be hidden behind list-keeping operations expressed in business terms.

items.name: Embedding-host volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: the environments that host the human-facing todo experience at the same moment: a plain browser for the web app, and the various MCP Apps hosts the team already embeds UIs into. WHY volatile: these hosts are not uniform today. They differ in sandboxing, available interactions (focus and blur, keyboard handling for Enter and Escape during edit), sizing, and how they hand the user's identity and actions back to the service. LIKELIHOOD: high. Every host the team uses differs now, and each host's capabilities change on its own release cadence. EFFECT if unencapsulated: host-specific quirks would leak into the todo workflows (for example, edit-commit-on-blur behaving differently per host), so the faithful TodoMVC behavior would differ by where it is embedded. Host adaptation must be confined to the presentation edge for each host.

items.name: Acting-party authority volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: which acting parties may act on a given owner's list. Today that is the owner, plus whichever agents act for that owner, keyed on the principal the platform supplies. WHY volatile: at any one time the team runs several different agent tools, and each is delegated differently. One agent may be trusted to act for a single team member, another for several. The mission requires agents to act 'on the same footing as people', which makes delegation, rather than identity, the open-ended rule. LIKELIHOOD: medium. The delegation arrangements change whenever a new agent workflow is wired up, which happens several times a year in agent-driven teams. EFFECT if unencapsulated: list-ownership checks would be scattered across every action and channel, and a change in delegation would require touching each one. Getting it wrong lets one member's agent change another member's list. Authority over a list must be decided in one place.

items.name: Cross-surface freshness volatility
items.rationale: WHAT: how a surface showing a list learns that the list was changed elsewhere. This covers an agent completing todos while the owner has the web app or an embedded MCP app open, or the same owner having two surfaces open. WHY volatile: the surfaces in use at any one moment differ in what they support. Some hosts allow pushed updates, others only refresh on request. Items left must reflect the true active count, and the list must be exactly as last kept. LIKELIHOOD: medium-high. As soon as agents drive lists (objective 4), concurrent changes from another surface are routine rather than exceptional. EFFECT if unencapsulated: each surface would invent its own refresh scheme, and stale counts and lists would appear inconsistently per host. The fix would ripple into every action that changes the list. This is expected to land as an operational concept (change notification) rather than a component.

rejected.name: Todo-attribute volatility (due dates, priorities, tags)
rejected.reason: The behavior contract explicitly puts due dates, priorities and tags out of scope and says they 'must not be assumed required'. A todo is a title plus a completed state, and encapsulating future attributes would be designing for a hypothetical product.

rejected.name: Manual-ordering volatility (drag-to-reorder)
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope. Todos are appended at the end of the list, and no stated ask or objective implies user-controlled ordering.

rejected.name: Change-history volatility (undo/redo)
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope. Cancel edit is the only 'undo' the contract asks for, and it lives inside a single edit, not as a history.

rejected.name: Offline-sync volatility
rejected.reason: Explicitly out of scope. The founder wants lists kept on the team's side, not on the device, which is the opposite of offline-first.

rejected.name: List-sharing volatility (multi-user lists)
rejected.reason: Multi-user sharing is explicitly out of scope, and the glossary fixes exactly one owner per list. Only agent delegation for that owner is grounded, and it is kept as Acting-party authority volatility.

rejected.name: Sign-in / identity volatility
rejected.reason: How team members and agents authenticate is already encapsulated by the platform's Security utility and front door (each op receives rc.Principal). Encapsulating it again would duplicate a utility, and this business is not identity.

rejected.name: Agent action-set divergence
rejected.reason: The mission mandates 'exactly the same todo actions to people and to the team's agents alike'. Designing for agents to get a different action set contradicts the stated mission rather than anticipating a grounded change.

rejected.name: Multiple-lists-per-owner volatility
rejected.reason: The glossary defines one todo list per owner, and no ask mentions projects or multiple lists. Encapsulating list multiplicity is might-need-someday design.

rejected.name: Reminder / notification block
rejected.reason: A siren-song block. Nothing in the brief or contract asks for reminders or alerts to team members, and the cross-surface freshness need is captured separately.

rejected.name: Reporting / activity-log block
rejected.reason: A by-reflex 'Reporting' or 'Logging' block with no business volatility behind it. No stakeholder asks for productivity reports or audit history.

rejected.name: Hosting / deployment-environment volatility
rejected.reason: The founder wants it built 'the way we build everything else here'. Where and how the service runs is the platform's fixed runtime doctrine, not a project volatility, so encapsulating it here would duplicate the platform.

rejected.name: Team-size / load volatility
rejected.reason: This is a small-team trial tool with one list per member, and no growth figures were stated. Scaling is handled by the platform's scaling policy, not by this system's architecture.

rejected.name: Bulk-change rules (toggle all / clear completed semantics)
rejected.reason: These follow the TodoMVC reference that 'many apps implement identically', and the mission says to reproduce it faithfully. Changing them would change the nature of the product, and any encapsulation would be poor.

rejected.name: Edit-outcome rules (blank edit discards, cancel restores)
rejected.reason: This is a fixed part of the TodoMVC contract every implementation shares. It is rare to change and is not meaningfully encapsulable beyond the edit workflow itself.

rejected.name: Filter-set volatility (All / Active / Completed)
rejected.reason: Filter matching is a predicate on the completed state. Even adding a filter is a conditional over data the todo already has, which is variable, not architectural.

rejected.name: Items-left counting rules
rejected.reason: Active counting is a count over the completed state of the whole list. Any tweak (for example pluralising 'item'/'items') is conditional logic.

rejected.name: Title-checking rules
rejected.reason: Treating empty or whitespace-only wording as blank, or adding a length limit, is a single validation conditional and does not ripple across the system.

rejected.name: Chosen-filter remembering
rejected.reason: Whether the chosen filter is remembered between visits is a small presentation choice handled by a flag or URL state on each surface.

rejected.name: Concurrent-edit conflict policy
rejected.reason: With one owner per list and single-todo changes, choosing last-writer-wins or rejecting a stale change is a conditional at the list-keeping seam. The open-ended part (how other surfaces learn of changes) is kept as Cross-surface freshness volatility.

rejected.name: Visual styling / branding
rejected.reason: Look and feel is styling within each presentation surface, adjusted by configuration and CSS rather than by architecture.

rejected.name: Machine-protocol volatility (web API vs MCP tools)
rejected.reason: This is the same underlying change as how parties reach the shared todo actions, so it is folded into Access-channel volatility.

rejected.name: Human-surface volatility (web app vs MCP App)
rejected.reason: Adding or replacing a human surface over time is the same change as Access-channel volatility. Variation across hosts at one time is kept separately as Embedding-host volatility.

rejected.name: Edit-gesture volatility (double-click, Enter, Escape, blur)
rejected.reason: How an edit is started, committed or cancelled differs only because hosts differ, so it is folded into Embedding-host volatility.

rejected.name: Storage-technology volatility
rejected.reason: This is the same underlying change as where lists are kept on the team's side, so it is folded into List-keeping volatility.

decisions.essenceRationale: Every todo act the customer named (add, retitle, discard, complete, reopen, toggle all, clear completed) is one business act: an authorised party changes one owner's kept list and the whole list stays true. That is what every team member and every agent buys, it is unchanged by which surface they use, which store keeps the list, or which agent is delegated, and it is the product. Each customer-named act is just a permutation of this one abstraction. It crosses the access-channel, acting-party authority, list-keeping and cross-surface freshness seams.

decisions.essenceRationale: Seeing exactly what is left to do, kept as it was left and viewed the way the owner prefers, is what every team member and agent relies on before acting. Without it, changing the list has no purpose. It stays the same whatever the surface, the host the view is embedded in, or the store that keeps the list, and it is what makes the tool trustworthy where a browser-only toy is not. Filtering, the items-left count and finding the list intact on return are all permutations of this one act. It crosses the access-channel, embedding-host, acting-party authority and list-keeping seams.

verdicts.summary:
REQUIRED

1. The refresh has nowhere to go (trigger honesty and realization truth). View `uc-refresh-an-open-surface` starts at the queued TodoListManager→TodoListManager "delivers ListChanged" and ends at `recallList`. The list the Manager recalls has no route to the team member's open surface. No edge reaches WebClient or McpAppClient (a Manager→Client call would be upward), and nothing lets a Client subscribe. So `show-refreshed`, and `announce-change` in `uc-work-the-list` ("let the owner's other open surfaces know"), promise a delivery the model cannot make. The self-queued ListChanged is drawn only to connect a chain. Give the delivery one real seam and draw it once. Either (a) add a pub/sub Utility that WebClient and McpAppClient subscribe to, with the publish as the single business edge (no duplicate M→M edge for the same act), or (b) keep the queued M→M root, add an explicit deferral of surface push to `.operationalConcepts` in the Manager's prose, and say in the `recall-list` fragment who receives the recalled list. Put Cross-surface freshness in the typed list of whichever component hosts the seam.

2. The same Manager operation is drawn at different granularities across views (cross-view symmetry). In `uc-work-the-list`, every change op (addTodo, rewordTodo, discardTodo, setTodoCompletion, toggleAll, clearCompleted) calls DecideAuthority, then the write, then `tallyList`, then the queued ListChanged. The variation views run the same ops with the same return contracts ("+ items left") and draw only the write:
   - `uc-add-a-todo` (`record-todo`), `uc-discard-a-todo` (`remove-todo`), `uc-complete-or-reopen-a-todo` (`set-completion`) and `uc-edit-a-todo-s-title` (`remove-todo` and `retitle-todo`) return items left but never call `tallyList`.
   - No variation view calls AuthorizingEngine, including the read views `uc-switch-the-filter`, `uc-see-how-many-todos-are-left` and `uc-come-back-to-the-list-later`. In `uc-review-the-list`, `listTodos` does call it.
   - No change variation announces ListChanged.
   The variation diagrams have no node of their own for these calls, but the calls belong in the existing fragments. Put DecideAuthority in the Client→Manager entry step, and `tallyList` (and the announce) after the write in the write step, so one op is drawn the same way everywhere. Alternatively, record why an op genuinely does less in a variation. Today the drawings disagree about what one operation does.

3. Access-channel volatility is filed in the wrong layer. TodoListManager lists "Access-channel volatility" in `encapsulatesVolatilities`, and RestApiClient and McpToolsClient home it too. In the committed rationale, the channel is "a thin, replaceable edge over one shared set of todo actions". The Clients contain that change. The Manager is the stable side of the seam: it does not encapsulate the change, it is protected from it. A channel volatility is not a workflow volatility. Remove it from the Manager's typed list and prose, and let the Manager claim what it really contains, the change-announcement workflow (Cross-surface freshness), consistent with item 1.

COMMENTS (no action required)
- RecordTodo, retitleTodo, removeTodo and recallList are close to CRUD. They are acceptable for this domain, but setCompletion and setAllCompletion could be named for their business meaning (complete or reopen).
- In `uc-review-the-list`, `recall-list` already filters while `compose-view` claims the filtering. Pick one place.
- `DecideAuthority(principal, …)` is fine: it carries rc.Principal into the committed delegation rule and does not design authentication.
- The name TodoListManager is a domain noun. It is tolerable, but consider naming it for its workflow once item 3 is fixed.
- Engine:Manager is 1:1, the layering is closed, and the four surfaces' static edges match the realizations.

authorizingEngine.title: authorizingEngine contract — decides whether the acting party may act on an owner's list

Act.description: Kind of act on the list; the complete set for this version. change: add, reword, discard, set completion, toggle all, clear completed. review: list under a filter, count items left, come back later.

AuthorityDecision.description: The one authority rule, decided from rc.Principal (platform-authenticated) plus owner and act. Permitted iff (a) rc.Principal.Subject is non-empty and equals owner (the owner acting on their own list, any act), or (b) the principal carries a delegation for owner in its platform-issued claims (claim actsFor: list of {owner, acts}) whose acts include act. People and agents (Principal.Kind user|application) go through the same rule. Everything else is refused: fail closed on empty owner, unknown act, malformed claims. Pure and deterministic: no I/O, no clock, no RNG, no global mutable state; safe to call directly from Manager workflow code. A refusal is a result, not an error.

OwnerID.description: Stable id of the list owner whose list the act targets (one owner per list). A business key, not caller identity: the acting party is always rc.Principal, never a parameter.

RefusalReason.description: none exactly when permitted. noActingParty: rc.Principal has an empty Subject. notActingForOwner: the principal is neither the owner nor delegated for the owner. actNotGranted: a delegation for the owner exists but does not cover this act (e.g. review-only). Coarse and for the Manager's log only; the surface shows a plain refusal and never learns whether the other owner's list exists.

authorizing-engine.content:
# AuthorizingEngine — Requirements (scope note)

**Layer:** Engine · **Contract key:** `authorizingEngine` · **Activity:** C-authorizing-engine

**Encapsulates:** *Acting-party authority volatility*. This component decides whether an acting party (the list owner, or an agent delegated to act for that owner) may act on a given owner's list. The volatility record explains why this needs one home. Delegation arrangements change several times a year as new agent workflows are wired up, and the mission requires agents to act on the same footing as people. If the rule were scattered, a change in delegation would touch every action and every channel. Getting it wrong would let one member's agent change another member's list.

## 1. Responsibilities (traced to the committed system design)

| # | Responsibility | Trace |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | Decide whether an acting **principal** may act on a given **owner's** list for a given kind of act, with exactly two outcomes: *permitted* or *refused*. | Relationship `todo-list-manager → authorizing-engine` (sync): "DecideAuthority(principal, owner, act) → permitted \| refused" |
| R2 | Decide authority for **changes** to a list: add, reword, discard, set completion, toggle all, clear completed. | Dynamic views `uc-work-the-list` (check-authority), `uc-add-a-todo` (check-title), `uc-edit-a-todo-s-title` (check-title), `uc-discard-a-todo`, `uc-complete-or-reopen-a-todo`, `uc-toggle-all-todos`, `uc-clear-completed-todos`. Each has the edge "DecideAuthority(principal, owner, change)" |
| R3 | Decide authority for **reviews** of a list: list under a filter, count items left, come back later. | Dynamic views `uc-review-the-list` (check-authority), `uc-switch-the-filter`, `uc-see-how-many-todos-are-left`, `uc-come-back-to-the-list-later`. Each has the edge "DecideAuthority(principal, owner, review)" |
| R4 | Treat the owner acting on their own list and an agent acting for that owner the same way, decided by one rule. People and agents reach the engine through the same Manager call, whatever channel they used. | Component `encapsulates`. All four clients reach the engine only through `todo-list-manager`. Glossary: "Agent" and "List owner" |
| R5 | Be the **only** place where list authority is decided. Neither the Manager nor any client nor ResourceAccess carries an ownership or delegation check of its own. | Volatility record "Authority over a list must be decided in one place". The engine is the single target of every check-authority step |

## 2. Callers / consumers

- **Sole caller: `TodoListManager`** (sync). It calls once per use-case execution, before any list-keeping call (`recordTodo` … `tallyList`). On a *refused* answer the Manager must not proceed to `TodoListAccess`. Acting on the outcome (stopping the workflow and reporting the refusal to the surface) is the Manager's job, not the engine's.
- **No other callers.** Clients must not call it (the Method forbids Client→Engine). ResourceAccess does not call it. Engines do not call each other.
- **Outgoing dependencies: none in the committed design.** The system has no relationship from `authorizing-engine` to any ResourceAccess, Resource, or other component. The engine does not publish or subscribe to `ListChanged`.
- **Inputs it relies on:** the acting **principal**, which the platform supplies through its Security utility and front door (`rc.Principal`; sign-in and identity were rejected as a project volatility because the platform already encapsulates them), plus the target **owner** and the **kind of act** (change vs review), both supplied by the Manager.

## 3. Non-functional constraints

**Security (primary quality bar)**
- **Fail closed.** Any principal, owner, or act the engine cannot positively establish as permitted must be refused. Missing, empty, or unrecognised inputs are never permitted.
- **No cross-owner leakage.** A principal permitted for owner A must be refused for owner B unless a delegation for B exists. This applies to reviews as well as changes, since reading another member's list is also a breach.
- **Never trust a caller-claimed identity.** The principal is the platform-authenticated one. The engine must not take on authentication or identity resolution; that belongs to the platform Security utility.
- A refusal must give no more information than needed. It should not reveal whether the other owner's list exists or what it contains.

**Maintainability**
- **Stateless and side-effect free.** The engine is a pure decision over its inputs plus whatever delegation knowledge it holds. It performs no list reads or writes and changes no state. That keeps it cheap to test exhaustively: owner-self, delegated agent, undelegated agent, wrong owner, and missing principal, each crossed with change and review.
- **Deterministic.** The same inputs and the same delegation arrangement always give the same answer.
- **No business-workflow logic.** Title checking, toggle-all direction, filter matching, and active counting belong to the Manager or ResourceAccess. They must not move into this engine.

**Extensibility**
- New delegation arrangements must be absorbable inside the engine, without changes to the Manager, the clients, or `TodoListAccess`. Examples: one agent acting for several members, or an agent scoped to review only.
- The change/review distinction is the act granularity the committed design uses today. A finer per-action distinction must not be assumed, but it should not be precluded either (see open questions).

**Performance / operability**
- The engine sits synchronously on every request path, so its decision must be fast and must not add a network round-trip to the existing per-request chain beyond the Manager's call.

## 4. Out of scope (explicitly)

- Authenticating team members or agents, and resolving identity. The platform Security utility does this.
- Multi-user list sharing, where one list has several human owners. This was rejected as speculative, and the glossary allows exactly one owner per list.
- Deciding the list's contents or validating titles.
- Surfacing or rendering the refusal to users. The Manager and clients do this.
- Notifying other surfaces. That is the Manager's `ListChanged` queued delivery.

## 5. Open questions for Detailed Design

1. **Source of delegation knowledge.** The committed system design gives the engine no outgoing relationship, so delegations cannot be read through a ResourceAccess. Detailed Design must settle where "which agents act for which owner" comes from without inventing a dependency. Candidates are claims carried on the platform-supplied principal, or engine configuration. If a delegation store is truly needed, that is an architecture change and must go back to the architect, not be added here.
2. **Owner identity.** How is the target *owner* established for a call? Is it always the principal itself for a human, and the delegating member for an agent? Or can a caller name an owner explicitly? This decides whether "self" is a trivial permit or needs checking.
3. **Act granularity.** The relationship label says `act`, while the dynamic views use only `change` and `review`. Confirm that these two kinds are the complete set for this version.
4. **Refusal shape.** Must a refusal carry a reason, such as "not delegated" or "no principal", for the Manager to log or map, given the security constraint of revealing as little as possible? Or is it a bare *refused*? Separately, how should a refusal differ from an engine failure (an error the engine cannot decide on)? Failure must still behave as *refused*.
5. **Agent vs person distinction.** Does the principal mark whether it is an agent or a person, or does the engine infer that from the delegation knowledge?
